utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while we're waiting for the witness, we have the video now, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have the video. We have two transcripts which I am myself reviewing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The video takes about 13 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm slightly undecided whether to deal with it through this witness or to deal with it through Dr. Loshi later in the week who is, I think, likely to be 92 bis'd for the most part but dealing with videos directly because there's the video of the bodies before they were buried that I think he's going to be dealing with quite probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more convenient when the accused will have had more time to prepare for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The only downside of that, to use a word I don't much like, is that I think it's this witness who interviewed the two Albanians, but then we have the fruits of his interview on the video. The alternative is for us to review the transcripts in advance because we can read them in less than 13 minutes and fast forward the video through the five seconds that show the broadcaster, the two Serbs pretending to be Albanians and the two Albanians, six segments, and the last segment showing the man carrying the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, so that may be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I distribute then in those circumstances the transcripts that I have. They're marked 1A -- very well. They're not marked 1A. They're in the same order that I have, so I'm going to take you through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the other problems about the transcripts is that we don't have English versions of all of it yet either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it was this witness who interviewed these people, then it's better obviously that he produces it so he can be asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's have the witness, please. Mr. Milosevic, you've got another ten minutes of your general cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped yesterday at the point, Mr. Xhemajli, when your explanation that you did not help the people who were about to be executed because you were afraid that you would jeopardise the civilians. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I helped people who had been injured, those who survived the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I asked you if it was true that you were watching somebody about to execute some people, and you, as the commander of a unit watching that from a wood, how is it that you didn't help them? How is it that you didn't try to prevent something like that, to prevent something like that from happening?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday because of the families of the people who were in the mass, in the group there. That's the reason. Because the families would have been jeopardised. There were 5.000 people in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were afraid that you would hit somebody from the families, is that true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was because of the families on the meadow. That's why we couldn't shoot, because of the families on the meadow, because -- it was because of you, because you had been holding all these families there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But couldn't you fire into the air in order to prevent this that you were about to witness, to prevent the event from happening? And you didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing. If we'd killed one policeman more or less, nothing would have changed. The execution would have taken place. There were children. There were women, old people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, are you supposed to tell this story in order to confirm the alleged charges and to conceal a crime? Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A NATO crime? Very well. This list here, based on what are you proving that this is a list of people who were killed and buried in Izbica, in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the leader of the people during the -- who buried these people, with certain friends. We all buried them together. I was there. I was a member of the committee for the funerals. I organised the recordings. We buried them all, and I was involved myself. I buried them with my own hands. And I identified them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is only a list of names here, and there is no proof for what you are claiming, but all right. Could you please tell me how much time you needed to ascertain that our forces had withdrawn from the Izbica region?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your forces withdrew on the 30th. They entered on the 27th, and at 9.45 on the 30th, they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There's obviously no point in wasting time on such questions because you will not respond to them. On page 7 -- on page 2 -- on page 7, paragraph 2, you stated that the money and the documents that were taken from the families were returned to them. When were they returned?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war ended. Some were returned during the war. Those who were found in the hills and nearby, they had their documents returned during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how is it possible that you found money when you previously claim that the soldiers confiscated all the money and the valuables? How did you find this money?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people had it hidden. Everybody had to give some. Your Honour, may I add something here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You explained that money was taken away from them and then you said that the money was found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now, what is it you want to say, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the -- this is money that was found in the pockets of people who were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We see that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We see that it is a banknote. Where it is found is something that we cannot see. Did you and your unit participate in the fighting which was conducted from the 24th to the 29th of March in that area?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can I take that as an affirmative response? What losses did your unit and the other units, the other brigades of the KLA, sustain in the period from the 24th to the 29th of March?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some. There were very few members of the units who were lost, but the populous lost -- had suffered many casualties, members of families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you stated yesterday in response to my questions that you had three brigades in that region, did you bury the participants in the fighting with our force -- with our soldiers and the police, or do you still claim that you buried civilians?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were. And you said that some man gave you land. Isn't it a custom in Kosovo that each family takes its kin rather than allow him to be buried somewhere else unless he's a soldier? Is this right or not, Mr. Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When people die in a natural way, they're all buried in their own graves. But these people were executed, and they must be buried at the place where they were executed. And soldiers who -- who come into danger and are -- meet their deaths that way are all buried together. They were all buried -- they were all killed together in the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean those who are killed in fighting are buried as soldiers? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said soldiers who put their lives in danger and who are killed through no fault of their own, who are executed, will be buried together. And I said this in my statement. Because some were killed in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe -- very well, yes. You claim that that is so, but I claim that each family wants to take its family member regardless of the way in which he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point arguing with the witness in this way. Now, you've got one more question left and then your time is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why only one? You said ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and you've had your ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe this mass grave where you buried them allegedly?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- the mass grave is long and -- along one side there is a stream, and Hamdi Bajrami granted the land for the martyrs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you bury them in separate graves or did you put them all in one grave?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where he granted the land, they were all buried separately on 28th of March. These were new graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic -- do you have any questions, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more questions, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've had your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have only a few matters that might assist the Court for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Witness, about your glasses, since when are these glasses prescribed by a doctor?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you wear glasses in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999? Yes, from September on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And were these glasses that corrected your sight?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is to shelter me from the light.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But the question was: Do they also correct your sight?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And what is the correction, for far-sight or for seeing nearby?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Short-sight. Now I can -- now I can see further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. Do you know the number or the percentage of correction?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I'm not a specialist in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: During the events in March 1999, am I right in thinking you did not wear glasses?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: About the KLA, when you joined the KLA, you were a private, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sure, but you were a private, not a ranked officer?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: During the war. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who was your commander when you joined the KLA? Unit commander, that is.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Until you were promoted yourself?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a list there in Kosova. All soldiers are entered into this register. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But you can say who was your commander when you joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All soldiers and their commanders are registered with UNMIK, both now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sure. But who was your commander when you joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Why can't you answer the question? It's a perfectly straightforward question, Mr. Xhemajli. There may be some reason you don't want to answer it. Instead of fencing with counsel, either answer it or tell us why you don't want you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I was the first leader of the squad, and I was the commander of a platoon myself, and he asks who my commander is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Court when you joined the KLA you were a private and later on you got promotion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First a group was formed, an ordinary one, and then we formed a group, a squad, and then the squad came -- became a platoon and I became the platoon commander. But every -- everybody starts as a private, as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you started as a private, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm explaining that I was myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He seems to be saying he didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you were commander of your unit, did you always stay with your -- with your unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you were watching on the 28th of March, 1999, what happened, can you describe the time frame? You told the Court when it all happened, it started with the Serb forces advancing about noon. When did it all happen? I mean, when did it all finish, on that late afternoon, beginning afternoon? Could you provide the Court with a time frame?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The departure of the family was -- they finished leaving at about half past one, and then they burned the tractors and the cars and the things that were left on the meadow, the livestock, and then they burnt the houses and everything else on the 28th of March. And they went on burning on the 29th. And at 9.45 in the morning on the 30th, the Serbian forces left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in the wood, in the woods, and you watched this all, were you on higher ground?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit, yes. Partly, yes. Slightly higher it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And where was your unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were they with you?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were rather further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by "further up"? Can you describe the distance?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 200 metres away behind a hill by a stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So they could observe you and you could observe them?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You were in contact with your unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I went myself on foot from time to time. We met every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They were on higher ground than you were, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were further up, but you couldn't see them. They were behind a hill. You had to go round.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there any obstacles --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the position where they are, you couldn't see anything. They couldn't see the execution or the meadows, and I went round the hill to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You told the Court there was a fight between the 24th and the 29th of March, is that right, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "fight."

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was it then? Your unit was engaged in any incident?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The order came from the higher command not to do anything because the family -- because of the families who were on the meadow and in case reprisals were taken, because we considered everybody there, including women and children, the elderly, we considered them all to be KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you report what happened on the 28th to your commander, higher commander?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by "later"?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we met in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So you were not instructed on the 28th itself by a higher command, were you?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th we were, because it was on the 27th that some of the families started going out onto the meadow. And on the 28th, the number grew when they came from other villages, from Citak, Padalishte, Lecina, Trnovo, Kastriot, Klladernica, and it became a great crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you report to higher command what happened on the 28th, what you watched?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you instructed how to deal with the matter?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No instructions of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How did you communicate with --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as the Serbian forces were there. Just to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And what were the means of communication with higher command?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had radio links; others did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you communicate yourself or through your unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only through the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So you were in contact with your unit that day, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the evening, after everything had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's all I ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have re-examination, but it might be more convenient to deal with that -- it's not very much, about half a dozen questions -- to deal with that all at the end rather after any questions of the accused when we've played the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we play the video then now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we have to play this 13 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court's happy to read the transcript first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that. We'll read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I sit down while the Court does that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Just a moment. We're reading this transcript. You can address us then. Mr. Nice, you first of all have to explain where this comes from, and next we'll have to consider the admissibility of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with it through the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, very briefly, the video that contains various components includes a television broadcast. Where did that come from? Who recorded it and when?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made in Switzerland by Mr. Rexhepi after the war. His brother gave a copy of it to me. And then I saw someone saying that the village of Izbica doesn't exist, there's only 12 houses, only 70 inhabitants, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. And then you saw on the same clip, was it, the two alleged Albanians denying that anything happened in the village of Izbica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two Serbs from the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all we need. Next thing is the composite video then contains interviews with the two -- with two people bearing the names of the names given by the people you say were Serbs. Was it you who conducted those interviews? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's clear from the transcript that you conducted the interviews after evidence had been given and broadcast by a woman witness here to whom denials of the incident happening at all had been put by the accused. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And roughly when did you conduct those interviews?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Albanians? I did them later, a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It sounds to me like rebuttal evidence. It doesn't sound to me like proper evidence in chief, but we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to exclude this document. At the moment, it is -- just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't -- just a moment. It does not relate to any issue which has been raised. It can be put forward in rebuttal if some issue is raised. It is made out by this witness, and we're not minded to admit it. That concludes the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make just two observations about that and then move on to the re-examination? The position is as I explained it yesterday, and as I explained yesterday, it may feature additionally as an element in relation to propaganda, so it may turn up there. Secondly, the Chamber said that the matter was in issue and thus the video became admissible. I was concerned yesterday that there may have been some misunderstanding as the purposes, so I'm quite happy to deal with it as a rebuttal issue. But I should say that it appears, and it's quite important that this should be clarified, that the accused still is denying that this issue occurred at all. It's not entirely clear to me whether he's running a second defence that it was in some way misdescribed or miscast. It seems to me he's challenging this killing occurred at all. Now, if that is the case, it would be helpful for us to know that in advance, and I don't want to take the accused by any -- by surprise, so I must tell the Court this: If he is really saying that this incident didn't happen at all, he hasn't challenged the reburial, that is, the taking of the bodies and their removal. We have material which I can't identify for reasons in detail at the moment which has led to a detailed request for assistance in relation to provision of the relevant report. That report has so far been denied us going to show what happened at the reburial, the taking of the bodies and their removal, and we will be seeking the assistance of the Court in due course to compel production of that report, but it's important for us to know whether the accused is denying that the incident happened at all and that there was thus no removal of the bodies as the material may in due course unequivocally confirm or whether he's offering some alternative explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you must take it in this case that you will get no assistance from him. You can take it that everything is in issue and every explanation is put forward, and if you deal with the matter on that basis, I think we'll get on as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I think we will be coming to the Court for further assistance in relation to this particular documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked that the booth play a very short clip in light of the cross-examination of a video that will be produced by Dr. Loshi later in the week, and I just want us to look at a very short of it and take the witness's answer on it. Yes, it's not the video we were originally looking at. It's a different video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a different video. We'll return the transcripts, if the Registrar would take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just play a short bit from it, but it won't be produced until Friday or whenever, but if we can have a look at it just now, please, Dr. Loshi's video as it will be. Right. Here it is. In due course, Mr. Xhemajli, Dr. Loshi will produce this exhibit. It's not moving very satisfactorily at the moment. Can it be made to advance a little? I don't want it as a still. I want it as a moving. Cut that. That's not the part we want. Dr. Loshi -- oh, here we are. This part here. Just look at this, please -- and let the video run, please, just for 30 seconds. Is this a video and a view you've seen before? Mr. Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the western side there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that just simply part of a video made of the bodies before they were buried? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused is effectively suggesting --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same place where the people were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll see all of that later this week or more of that later this week. The accused is suggesting that you have simply made up this entire account of people being killed, lying in a field, and being buried. Have you made it up or is what you've told this Tribunal true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the original. That's where the people were executed. No one was -- none of the bodies were moved at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a number of questions have been asked about the accused's -- the witness's statement. May the statement be produced as an exhibit? That deals with the problem of the two lists to which I referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have a number for it before we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecutor's number 287.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't need to look at it any further but as you explained to the learned Judges yesterday, did you identify in your statement people who survived as eyewitnesses to this massacre? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course the Tribunal will know as will those following the trial that two such witnesses have already been called. You were taken -- perhaps I just ought to ask you to have a look at -- no. I'll ask the Tribunal to look at -- speed. You were taken on page 3 in the English version of your statement to a sentence that began "On the 24th of March". And only a couple of sentences were read to you. It was read that "On the 24th of March, NATO commenced its offensive against Serbia. It was very welcome at this time. The KLA wasn't so strong then and needed help." That was read out to you. What was not read out to you but was in your statement has the immediate following sentence was as follows: "The Serbs were killing civilians, women and children. Some KLA soldiers were killed protecting their families." Were those two sentences in your statement true? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. They killed children. And there were conflicts which were not caused by -- by our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's been suggested to you by the accused either that your story is false or effectively he's saying you were showing lack of courage in not going down and intervening in what you may have foreseen at the time as a developing crisis that could have led to killings. What do you say to the suggestion that it was lack of courage that led you down there, that stopped your going down there to intervene in this field of thousands of people? What do you say to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before it's not true that we couldn't act. We could have acted to protect our families. But we knew what was going on. There were crimes being committed, and we want didn't -- for that reason, we didn't want to jeopardise all our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The allegation includes effectively that you've made up everything that you've said and that the bodies didn't exist and that people weren't killed. You've explained to this Tribunal that you made your list that we've seen from notes. The notes that you made, were they contemporaneous and by "contemporaneous" I mean --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were contemporaneous, yes. At the same time, at the same time people were being buried everyone was registered that time when they were being buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you please take from your bag the book that we know you don't want to hand over permanently but you say contains your original notes? I'm going to ask you to show it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we can have it photocopied in its original form and made an exhibit if the Judges so decide.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will just have a look at the format of these notes that you say were original, prepared at the time that you were dealing with the bodies that were buried, so that the Judges can see it?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it here, these pages. Not that one but all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I ask Your Honours to look at this. I'll arrange to have it photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough pages. They only need to see a sample. Thank you. Hand it in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Show it to the accused. Just those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's being -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness, would you just -- Witness, will you listen to me for a minute? While that's being done, would you just get ready to hand to me the photographs of yourself at various gravesites that I've seen and I may just want to show to the Judges in light of one of the items of cross-examination? No, don't take them out of -- no, don't take them out. Leave them in there. No. It's the one of you at the gravesites. It's the other album.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before we get to this, would you take the notebook back so that you can have it photocopied? We'll see that in a moment, Mr. Xhemajli. Take the notebook back. You can photocopy the relevant pages. We will take now, so that we have it in sequence, an exhibit number for those pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 288.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't hold them up, Mr. Xhemajli. Can you hand all those photographs to me, those photographs and the other album that shows you at various cemeteries, please. There's another album that shows you at various cemeteries. Can you just hand them to me, please? Thank you. Thank you very much. A suggestion -- questions have been asked about your use of dark glasses. Is this album, which by probably doesn't need to be produced, an album of photographs of you at various gravesites since the war? Can you just show it to Their Honours, please? Your Honours, the point of this is extremely obvious. If you look at the photographs, they all contain a picture of the witness. They all contain him wearing dark glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't swear to it, Your Honour, but I think every one has him with dark glass on. I don't ask it to add to the burden of exhibits in the case once they've been seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show it to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can you tell us please, Mr. Xhemajli, over approximately what period of time, what years were those photographs taken?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones you have in your hands, they were taken at the time when the people were buried in May, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, the ones I've just shown to Their Honours of you at various cemeteries, when were they taken?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war. They were taken after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other two photographs you've handed to me were taken when?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of May, the day of the burial. We buried the people on the 12th, the people who had been executed. They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Give these to Their Honours, and my last question. These are two photographs that the witness happens to have, although I think the exhibits of Dr. Loshi will be much more comprehensive generally. And, Your Honour, again I don't ask that we burden the exhibit list or the store of exhibits with these photographs, but they're two photographs that this witness happens to have in his possession in support of his testimony. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the tape, Mr. May, first of all, I have an objection. And secondly, I have to ask him about this tape that was actually played now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've -- which tape are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last night, with my very own eyes, precisely because of these manipulations by Mr. Nice, I saw on television --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will stop this. You will stop making these wild allegations of manipulation. There is no foundation for them at all. Now, you will conduct yourself as though you're in a Court. Now, that -- that tape has been ruled out. Any re-examination was perfectly proper on that limited basis which it was allowed in. I'm going now to ask this witness to withdraw, his evidence having finished. We are not admitting the other tape. You know that. So there's no point in you going on about it. No. We've had enough on this point. Mr. Xhemajli, would you withdraw, please? We've heard your evidence. Thank you for coming. We're going on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you. I would like to thank you, Your Honours, and international justice for persecuting [As interpreted] crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution called Musa Krasniqi as the next witness. Again, Your Honours. I believe that according to a ruling, the request was that the Prosecution not proceed by way of 92 bis with respect to this witness, but proceed with him as a witness viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealing with a new area, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There will be other witnesses who are the subject of an application for 92 bis, but he is the first to speak about Dubrava Prison. And while we're waiting, if Your Honours wish to look at the atlas, page 5. Page 5. The best way to describe the location would be you see at line 60 at the top and line -- well, 12 on the side, and then you'll see the big village of Istok and about an inch to the right of that you see Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I understand, sir, that you're a 40-year-old Kosovo Albanian from Barane in the municipality of Peja in west Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From Barane, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, sir, I understand as well that you're married, you have a son, and your occupation is that of a teacher of physics in a local village school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it also true, sir, that you completed your military service in the JNA in 1983 with an artillery unit based in Knin in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: During 1998, sir, were you a KLA member and a commander in the Barane KLA headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to start telling us, if you would, please, about events that happened on the 11th of September of 1998. On that date, did something happen to you that caused you eventually end up being institutionalised in a prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 11th of September, I fell into an ambush. That is not really a police checkpoint but an ambush. And the Serbian police, after stopping me, sent me to the police station in Peja, and there they held me for 24 hours, and I was interrogated by two people. One of them I knew. We had completed the faculty in the same building. He had been a teacher of geography while I was a physics teacher. And after 24 hours, they sentenced me to three days. And then on the 17th of September, I came in front of an investigating Judge. And on the 27th September, they sent me to Lipjan prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, sir, after you were being interrogated by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one of these who had been a faculty colleague of yours, do you know why you were being interrogated and why you were sent to prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They had information that I had been a commander in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And -- now, you say that you were held -- eventually you were sent to Lipjan prison in the latter stages of September 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Had you yet had a trial or were you awaiting trial? Were you on remand status?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were waiting for our trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. What happened once you got to Lipjan?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were waited by cordons of prison wardens and policemen who maltreated us incessantly for five days. And then after five days, we were in danger from hunger, and then we were given 500 grams of bread for five people. That's 100 grams each. And then they started maltreating us now and then, not collectively. And I was kept there until the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now -- so it was the 5th of December that you were transferred somewhere else, I take it. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On 5th of December, they took me to Dubrava Prison near Istog.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, the prisoners at Lipjan prison with whom you were incarcerated, do you know what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. We were all Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do you happen to know the ethnicity of the guards or the prison officials who were looking after the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were some Albanians, but we couldn't really -- unable to see them. They were forbidden to contact us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Anyway, when you got to Dubrava on the 5th of December, 1998, where were you placed?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When we came to Dubrava, I was put in the isolation block known as C block. And when I went up to the first floor, there were about 56 other prisoners, and there were about 108 brought from Lipjan, and they were put on other floors as well as in the isolation blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you were not the only prisoner brought from Lipjan. You were there with a group of others also transferred to Dubrava on the 5th of December, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As I said, there were about 108 of us who were transferred from Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you place this photograph on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now, sir, what appears to be an aerial photograph of the Dubrava Prison. Have you seen that photograph before? Do you recognise the scene depicted in that particular photograph, sir? Is that a photograph of Dubrava Prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at tab 4 of Exhibit 165, the Dubrava binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is Dubrava Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. You said you were placed in C block, in the isolation area. Perhaps with a pointer or whatever else Madam Usher can find for you, you can show us on the ELMO what building you were placed in when you first got there. If you point on the ELMO, then we can see it on the television screen. Can you reach forward and show us? Lean forward so we can also get your voice in the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This is C block, the isolation block.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's where you went when you arrived. All right, sir. How many prisoners do you -- do you recall how many prisoners were in C block altogether?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: About 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And were there other prisoners in other buildings within the Dubrava Prison compound?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were a very few who of people who had been sentenced to long sentences of years for murders and ordinary crimes but not many of them. But we in the isolation block, we were on remand, under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were people on remand housed generally separately from people who were there serving a sentence after being convicted?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of your stay at Dubrava from December 5th to, say, early May of 1999, did more prisoners arrive at the prison? And if so, do you know what the total was by early May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After I was sentenced on 16th March and after the start of the NATO bombing, round about -- from the beginning of April to 3rd of May, they brought all the prisoners to the Dubrava Prison from all the prisons of Serbia. So by this time we were about 224 of us. And after the 3rd of May, we were more than 930 because of the people that they brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know -- did you have any -- while you were at the prison, did you notice the presence of any military installations around the perimeter of Dubrava Prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tell us about that. What do you know was there and how do you know it?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Dubrava Prison is on a slope, and you can see here the area outside the perimeter wall where there were military columns in movement, changing place time after time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where? Are you able to describe by pointing at the photograph the areas where you saw these military columns? Is that visible? Just point that out with a pen if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It's not really very visible, but near the administrative block here. And this was -- you could also conceal military equipment here where I'm pointing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You're, for the record, pointing to the top end of the photograph behind the word "Admin block" on the photograph. Did you actually see any military equipment apart from columns, troop columns?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We saw APCs and tanks and anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of those military equipment facilities in operation? For example, did you ever see the anti-aircraft guns being used?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the day when they -- they took us out to Lipjan the second time, when I left the prison gate I saw these anti-aircraft guns destroyed by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Prior to seeing them destroyed, had you ever seen them being fired? And by "fired" I mean that they were shooting at something with them.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Round about April, they provoked the NATO aeroplanes by using these anti-aircraft guns for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say "provoked," what actions did you see that caused you to believe that it was provoking? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I heard a guard near my window saying that, "It seems to me that they all hit the aircraft."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you hear the guns being shot, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. They were firing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, either from your own knowledge or from what you heard from others, do you know whether Dubrava Prison had been used for any other purpose other than a prison before your arrival on the 5th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Before we came, Dubrava Prison was used for logistics purposes by the Yugoslav army. There was generally Serbian forces there, soldiers, policemen, and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, just a few moments ago in response to another question, you indicated that you had been moved to another location after your trial. When was your trial and what were you convicted of?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The trial was held on 16th of March, 1998 [As interpreted], and I was sentenced on the -- supposedly as a member of the KLA and an activist of the Democratic League of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if I misheard you or whether it was a translation problem, but I heard the interpretation that you were convicted on the 16th of March, 1998. Do you mean 1998 or 1999 that you were convicted?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I mean 16th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your sentence for those convictions?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was sentenced on the accusation, on the charge of terrorist conspiracy as a member of the KLA and a member of the Democratic League of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question must not have been clear. How long was your sentence? Like how much time were you sentenced to serve for that conviction?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was sentenced to one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And where were you sentenced to serve that one year? Was that back at Dubrava Prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After the verdict, they -- they took me immediately to Dubrava where I was to serve my sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, were you placed back in the same C block that you had been while you were on remand or were you placed in another building? And if so, is that building shown on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was put in the same building and stayed for four days on the second floor. And after four days, they eased my conditions as a sentenced prisoner and I was put on the ground floor in the same building by the entrance, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you were sentenced on the 16th. Did something happen on the 24th of March, 1999, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, at about twenty past eight in the evening, we heard a plane flying at great speed, and five minutes later, the guards came and they turned out all the lights and locked all the doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you subsequently hear from other prisoners who had had contact with people from outside what had occurred on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, at about 10.00, there was somebody whose name I cannot remember, a lawyer visiting his client, and he said that the Rambouillet conference had not been successful and that the NATO bombing would start that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move ahead, sir. First of all, on the 24th of March, 1999, did the attitude of the guards towards the prisoners change in any way?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the -- on the next day -- not on the 24th, but on the next day things started changing. There was -- there were fewer meals, less food. There was only two meals a day instead of three. And a few days later, the mishandling, the mistreating started, the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to skip ahead if I may to the 19th of May, 1999. What happened on that day that brought you to the court to talk about that today?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, at about 12.00 or 1.00 - we didn't have the right to wear watches - but it was round about midday, we heard a loud explosion in the prison complex on the administration building, and that is when a NATO bomb fell. After about five or six seconds, bombs fell on C block, two of them, and another one nearby or alongside it. On this occasion, we didn't really know what was happening. The guards fled and left us locked up in the prison. We started to break down the doors to get out of the cells. This was round about 1.30. Then other former prisoners who came who were now free, and they helped us to get out of the isolation block. Then on the second floor known as the hall, three prisoners died and 15 were injured by the bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. How many bombs did you say that fell in total on the 19th of May, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I believe that in all, four bombs fell. One on the administrative block, two on C block, and another one on the block alongside, nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, just so that we're clear, on the photograph that's on the ELMO before you, the administrative block is shown in the top left-hand corner. Would you look at it, please? Point that out.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. And there are two C blocks. One is C block isolation 12, and then when you look to the right of the photograph, there is C block 8 for convicted. Which block did the bombs fall on when you say they landed on C block?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Here on number 11. Two fell on 12 and one on 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So when we're talking about C block, you're talking about the isolation block at the lower part of the photograph and cell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. block 11 is one just to the north of it on the photograph. Thank you. All right. Now, two days later, sir, was the prison again bombed by -- was the prison again bombed?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On 21st of May, at about half past ten, the prison complex was bombed again. On this day, the guards and the prison administration were put us all in the yard what we called -- what we called the yard of the prison complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And you're pointing that out. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After awhile, the bombing started and the bombs -- the first bombs fell on the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Prison kitchen. And the second one fell on the reception block where there were 167 prisoners from Gjakove who had been taken as hostages. And they were told to leave the building and join us on the open space. But they said it's better to stay inside and be killed by NATO than to be massacred by the Serbs. And throughout that day there was further bombing of the prison complex, including what we called the sports hall or the gym, which is here. And all the other buildings were also hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One more question before I anticipate there will be a break, sir. Do you know how many prisoners were killed on the 21st of May as a result of that bombing?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: More than -- more than 16 were killed on 21st May. So if you join that to the other nine, there are 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move into the next topic which is of a different nature. I wonder whether this is the appropriate time for the break. I can start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, it would obviously be helpful if we had a copy of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Do Your Honours -- I believe Your Honours should have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In the tab. And while I'm thinking of it. I'm bad for housekeeping matters, I don't think I've asked for a number for the exhibit that's on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, see if you can make a better copy for us than the one we've got. It's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure whether Your Honours -- yeah, you have a different one. I'll have a copies of this one made. The ones Your Honours have in the binder are ones that I will show to the witness later. Those are ones in which he's actually -- it's similar but not identical. Those are the ones where he's actually made handwritten notations. I'll be referring to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those are attached to the statement which we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. What I will do is during the break is provide copies of the actual exhibit that I'm asking to have marked as a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And so I've got the evidence right, he's saying there were 23 killed, is that right, on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's what I heard him say, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Tab 4, Exhibit 165, I believe, should have a copy of the document that is on the ELMO now. It's different than the one attached to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be much easier if we started again with some good copies, if you could try and make them, and we will give it a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly will. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krasniqi, don't speak to anybody about your evidence during the adjournment, please, and don't let anybody speak to you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, just before we move on to the 22nd of May, I want to just ask you a couple of questions of clarification. I believe you told us about the number of people killed by NATO bombing. You did some math and ended up with 23. I understand you told us 16 were killed on the 21st. Where did -- I'm sorry. How did you get to 23? You added nine. Where were the nine? Was that on the same day, the 21st, are you talking about the 19th? Perhaps you could clarify that for us. You're getting no translation. All right. Let me try that again. Is the witness getting translation at the moment? Apparently not. I started before the booth was ready. Sorry. All right. Mr. Krasniqi, I believe you told us just before the break that you added nine people to a total of 16 prisoners that you say were killed on the 21st of May. Can you tell us where those -- where you get the figure of nine? Was that nine other prisoners killed on the 21st or are you referring back to the 19th? Perhaps you could tell us who you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 21st of May, there were 19. And then three were killed on the 21st and there were a total of 23 people who were killed during NATO bombings. And there were nine others on the 23rd of May who were killed. But we haven't spoken about them yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's still not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll do this piecemeal, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's start with the 21st of May. Mr. Krasniqi, would you please be very careful and listen to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the 21st of May, to your knowledge, how many people were killed as a result of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nineteen prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, two days earlier, you told us there were three killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I now want to move, if I may, to the -- we're trying to do this chronologically. On the 22nd of May, so the following morning after the second NATO bombing, I ask you to turn your mind to an event that occurred about 6.30 in the morning. Tell us in as much detail, please, what occurred on the 22nd of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On that date at 6.30 [As interpreted] in the morning, we'd been on the sports field under the open sky that night, the night before, a policeman came with a megaphone and turned to us from the watchtower of the prison and said that we were going to -- "We're going to take you out to Nis, to Nis Prison, for your own security." Then because of the bitter experience that former prisoners, Albanian prisoners had had in the Nis Prison earlier, we said that we should burn or destroy all our personal documents because the warden -- the prison guards would beat us and treat us very badly. So that's what we did. At about 6.00, the same person and two assistant guards turned to us and spoke through the megaphone once again saying that, "You have another ten minutes to get in line, to get ready."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask you to clarify something. I believe you indicated that you were asked to line up about 6.30 and then you said later at 6.00 they spoke to you again. Maybe you could clarify the times for us. Maybe I misunderstood you. What time were you first addressed through the megaphone and what time was it you were told you were going to be transferred to Nis Prison in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They woke us at 5.30, the same person with the megaphone. And then at 6.00 -- and then the rest was at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, eventually did the prisoners line up on the sports field?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We started lining up in about five or six lines of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How many men in total would you estimate were lining up in front of the watchtower on the sports field?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, the prisoners started lining up and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. My question is: Are you able to give us a numerical estimate as to how many men were lining up?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Over 800, because some of the prisoners went into hiding in the prison complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Then what happened, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After they told us to line up for the second time, it wasn't more than five seconds after that that grenades started falling. Hand grenades were thrown, four or five, and then there were hand -- there were bazookas, hand rockets, and all sorts of light arms, semi-automatic rifles, rifles, machine-guns started firing at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: At whom were they firing?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were firing at us who were in lines as we were lining up from all the walls of the prison and especially the parts of the walls which had been broken by NATO bomb. There were guards there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, during the break we do have copies of the exhibit. Have they been distributed to Your Honours? We do have those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 289.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I might say, Your Honour, although it's been given a number, you are aware it's already got Exhibit 165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking at the new exhibit that's on the ELMO, can you tell us, sir, is the watchtower visible on this particular exhibit? When you look at the sports field, is the watchtower shown on this exhibit or is it off the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The watchtower should be down here somewhere. And on the first copy you can see it, but not on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have also made a notation on another angle of this aerial photograph. Might I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can I ask you to place this on the ELMO? I believe this is the copy that's attached to the statement, Your Honour, but it shows the location. I apologise for the very poor quality of this document but it's the best copy we have. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recognise that document and have you attached your initials to it?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, just so that we can orient ourselves in relation to what this document is, at the top of the photograph we see the word "watchtower," and just below it we see an area called "sport field," I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And just so that we're clear, that is the same sport field as shown on the bottom right-hand corner of the previous exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So we're really looking at this document in a -- in a -- from a different viewpoint. Now, can you tell us where the men were lined up in relation to the document that's now on the ELMO and where the shooting was come from? Can you just explain that with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Here is the sports field and this is the tower, the tower where the guards were standing. And the lines were along this line, as far as that building, and the shots came from the watchtower and also from this perimeter wall and the other side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And as a result of the shooting as you've described, what happened to the men that were lined up in front of this watchtower?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Most of us didn't know -- didn't know what was happening, but some began to stretch out on the ground because they realised that the Serbs had started to kill us. And there were 97 people left killed and 157 wounded, and many others also died because of lack of medical care.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How long did the shooting by the guards from the wall and the watchtower, how long did that go on, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were two stages. First stage was with grenades, and then the second stage was with machine-gun firing. It was about ten minutes. And when they changed, their rifles changed, their cartridges, we tried to hide in the corners over there. It was about ten minutes altogether. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps you could describe to us what you did. You were on the sports field lined up in front of the watchtower as well, were you?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I was about over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you're now pointing to the right-hand corner of that rectangle referred to as "sports field," for the record. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Then I went in this direction near block C and down to the sports complex here with a few -- a couple of friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How were you able to leave this area where the shooting was going on? How were you able to escape?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Because of my experience in the Yugoslav army during military service and my experience during the war as a KLA soldier, I knew that when cartridges are changes -- when cartridges are changed, there's a small gap, and I used that gap to escape to other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the shooting resume during that lull that you talked about while cartridges were being changed? Did they start shooting again?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They started again but at random.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And where were they shooting from when they started again?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From the same direction but also from the other watchtowers that were situated at the other corners of the prison complex and which you can't see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Where did you go? You've told us you went to -- towards C block and then you eventually ended up in an area that I can't read on the photograph. What block -- where did you go? There's a building marked "Theatre," and you went down below that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Went in the direction of C block, and then there's a paved road by the theatre, and I reached the enclosed sports hall marked "gym."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. You went to the gym. Did you see where any of the other prisoners that survived, did you see what they did?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We all escaped in different directions among these buildings which were used as kind of shields from the firing from the watchtowers that were on all four sides. So we hid behind the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How long did you hide? You say this started at about 5.30 to 6.30 in the morning of the 22nd of May. After this incident of shooting, what did you do for the balance of the day?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We helped wounded prisoners, and round about 1.00 to 2.00, we went to the scene of what had happened and we lined up the dead bodies and we took away several others who were lying wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were killed during that shooting incident in the early morning hours of the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At this time, a total of 97 were killed according to my friend who counted them, and these included prisoners who had been convicted for common crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go further, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you say you were able to notice a small gap during which the cartridges were being changed; is that right? Then does it mean that there was only one person who was shooting at you at that time? From the watchtower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were a big group, and we all knew each other because we came from the same area. And when the cartridges were being changed, we shouted to each other and said, "You've got time. Move." And so from my -- on the basis of my experience, I knew that I had time to escape during that short interval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To your memory, how many people, how many persons were shooting against you, to your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very hard for us to see all of them who were shooting. But in the watchtower there was one older guard and two on either side of him. And from the gaps opened by the NATO bombings, you could see the barrels of automatic rifles pointing at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may just follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you able, sir, to give an estimate as to how many people in total would have been shooting at you? Was it a single source? Was it three? Was it 15? Are you able to give us a rough estimate of the number of people who were firing at the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Must have been about 20 if not more, because during the night when we slept on the open sports field, we heard a tractor moving in that area and no doubt it brought ammunition. And there was one fire, one shell from a Zolja which landed in the region by the theatre, and we heard a voice in Serbian saying, "Don't fire any more."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This Zolja you're referring to, is that a type of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A Zolja is a kind of weapon which has the form of -- resembles a hand-held rocket launcher. I don't know what other meaning it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. All right, sir. Now, you've told us that you and a number of prisoners hid. Can you tell us, did you -- did you hide overnight, or what happened the following day?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: During the night, about 315 prisoners, that's some of us, spent the night in C block which had been the isolation block and had been bombed, and the remainder stayed in the basement of the kitchen. And during the night, we organised some self-defence because we were scared that worse might happen and we might be massacred at close range. So we prepared various things that we found there, and from these resources we prepared some self-defence. So we got bed legs and window frames, ropes, scythes, and got these ready for the morning. And at about 5.30 in the morning, a group came in, a group of Serbs from the army, the police, paramilitaries, from different formations, and they started to open the drains that were used for sewage, and they threw in grenades down those manholes and shot those who had taken shelter there and sometimes shooting them in the back. And then they got to the kitchen and also started throwing hand grenades into the kitchen. And after awhile they forced these people to surrender, to put their hands behind their heads and to come to the sports hall. Then they sent two prisoners to C block who told us that we had to surrender within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, these people that were in the drains and in the kitchen, were these some of the prisoners who had earlier been on the sports field when they had been fired upon?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
