utterances.text: The same people who had been lined up, we split up 315 to C block and the remainder over here to the kitchen to take shelter during the night. So these were the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So the effect of the grenades being thrown in and these people being shot, were more people killed to your knowledge as a result of this action of the early morning hours of the 23rd of May, 1999? Did these people die from that?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Several people died from these grenades. Several people in the basement of the theatre where 22 people had been hiding. It's a very elaborate cellar area which was used for plumbing and for the -- there was a boiler room and there was piping for heating. And of these 22 people, nine people were executed at close range, stood up against a wall. And one of these people I knew. His name was Zef Kciraj and Hile Kciraj, had been in the same cell as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, after this incident -- well, perhaps -- you left off telling us that you were given a certain amount of time to surrender. Did the prisoners in fact surrender and if so where were you taken and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From C block they sent two prisoners from the kitchen to C block telling us to surrender and to come with our hands behind our heads to the sports hall where we were all rounded up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And once you were all rounded up, were you told anything by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were all rounded up in the sports hall and then some Serbian journalists came, and a Greek journalist. I don't know which television station or news agency he came from. And they counted the bodies and said that this is what NATO had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What bodies were being counted by whom and who said this is what NATO had done? Perhaps you could take that in steps. I understand there's a sort of press conference for some Serbian journalists and a Greek journalist. So far correct? First of all, can you tell us how many bodies? How many people had died?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, if you know, how many people had died as a result of both the shooting on the sports field and the incident the next morning when they were flushing people out of drains and out of the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: About 153 people were killed in the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, at this news conference, for lack of a better phrase, who indicated that this is what NATO had done?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Serbian policemen and guards who had come with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were these bodies, i.e., the people from the sports field and people killed the following morning, were they seen by these journalists?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They -- everybody saw them that day. That's on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, the following day, sir, the 24th of May, 1999, what happened to you? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After that, they enclosed us in the sports hall and said that they would take us to Smrekovnica Prison near Mitrovica or to Lipjan Prison. And the next morning, 6.00 in the morning, they lined us up and put us into eight buses with the wounded in four trucks, and they sent us off to the village of Dubrava which near Istog and then on to Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you served the balance of your sentence at Lipjan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We stayed 17 days in all in Lipjan, until 10th of June, when NATO started to enter Kosova, according to the agreement. And in June, they took us to Nis Prison where I stayed a further three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, did you personally know any of the people that were killed by the Serb forces either on the sports field or the following morning when they were throwing grenades into the drains and shooting into the kitchen and basement? Did you know any of the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I knew several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you by memory able to tell us some of the names of the people that were killed or would it assist you -- would you recognise names on a list as to some of those people? Are you able to remember by -- without looking at a list?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I can remember more surnames than first names. It would be a great help if I did have a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a blank list that I propose to show and ask the witness whether he recognises any of the names of the people that he knows who have been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The list is the same list as in Schedule J.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's going to be proved by somebody else, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm simply ask this witness as to how many names that he knows from this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll do it this way. I'll ask him to go by memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now I understand, sir, that you don't know all the first names. Can you tell us from memory how many of these names that you recall of people that were killed by the Serb forces on the 22nd and 23rd of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I can remember -- the following people were killed by NATO: Fadil Bezeraj from Rasic near Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you know those names. I'm now asking you to tell us the names of the people who were not killed by NATO, the people that were killed as a result of the Serb forces. I appreciate that you also know the names of the people who died from -- by NATO, but that's not my question at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The -- Sahit Ibrahimaj from Kotradiq in Peja municipality was killed by Serbian forces and also Agim Elshani from the town of Klina, Zahir Agushi from the town of Klina. Zek Hasan Metaj from the village of Strelce in Decan municipality. Iber Gogaci from the village of Kosuriq near Peja. And there were various other names that have slipped my mind at the moment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't -- didn't intend this to be a memory test for the witness. I would propose to show him a list and ask whether he recognises any names unless Your Honours feel that would be inappropriate to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only point is that clearly these matters are going to be disputed. How do the Prosecution propose to prove the number of people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There will be other witnesses as well who are going to testify as to what they say and will be adding other names to this process, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show him the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Actually, the list I want to put on?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Zahir Agushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's somebody you mentioned already?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Avni Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Zef Kciraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's somebody you mentioned earlier in your evidence before you were shown the list.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Valentin Nikoll Bibaj. Dervish Sylaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are those the names that you recognise, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: These are people that I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe those are my questions at this time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is manipulation here today and yesterday about tapes of an alleged execution that obviously did not take police and, Mr. May, you denied me the opportunity to respond to such manipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you wish to ask this witness any questions or not? If you do, you should cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You claim you were arrested on the 11th of September, 1998. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were sentenced to 12 months imprisonment. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were you sentenced for, for what criminal act?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was sentenced according to the penal law 125 of the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that you were sentenced as an alleged member of the KLA, and from the information which you provided yourself, is it true not only that you were a member of the KLA but also the commander of the headquarters for Barane? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was commander at the military base in Gorak [phoen] barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it cannot be said that you were sentenced because of something that you allegedly were but because of something that you actually were. As a member and a commander of the KLA staff, did you organ participate in terrorist acts against our forces, soldiers, police officers, and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't take part in any activities of the KLA. I was in the military barracks, and I assisted in the logistics for the KLA and in training cadets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as commander of the KLA headquarters in Barane were not involved in KLA activities. You did not take part in any fighting. Is that what you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't take part in any fighting. I was only involved in training new young cadets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you trained the newly recruited members of the KLA. Was that your job?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Out of those people that you trained, how many of them took part in the killings of soldiers, police officers, and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Some of them were involved in organised actions, activities. Some of them were guards. Some were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many of them lost their lives in these actions that you mention?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: None of my soldiers lost their lives in actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were released from prison, was that exactly at the point when you had served your 12-month sentence?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you released from prison? What date were you released?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 11th of September, 1999, from Nis Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were arrested on the 11th of September, 1998, that means that you spent one year in prison exactly to the day, which was the amount of your sentence. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that you were severely sentenced for that act since the punishment for that act that you were convicted of can be up to 15 years, but you were sentenced just to one year.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Investigating judge, judges, were not able to go to the site to collect information, where I was and where the members of the KLA were. So we were convicted of collaboration with the KLA and of being members of the LDK, of the Democratic League of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that they were not able to prove all of the things that you actually committed? Is this true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They didn't have any proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you can see here that these proofs are now obvious. Can you tell me how many projectiles NATO fired on the Dubrava Prison on the 19th of May? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Altogether four projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the 19th of May, 2002 [As interpreted]. That was the first day that the prison was bombed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's been a mistranslation. It must have been 1999. Or a misreference. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, of course. 1999. Perhaps it was my mistake. Maybe I said 2002. Perhaps the translation is not mistaken, but in any case, we all know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So may I have an answer?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As I said, there were four projectiles altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people lost their lives on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Three people lost their lives and over 15 were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me how you as an inmate in prison, which as we could see in this diagram is quite a large prison, can know precise information about the killed, the wounded, and so on? How did you have the possibility to see all this, to find out, to hear, and to count everything?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have a bit of experience, ten years of experience with the Democratic League of Kosova, from 1991 on, and I have education to be able to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if my question is clear to you. You're a prisoner. How were you able to freely move about the prison, to count, and to determine exactly what was going on in the prison? Does that mean that you could move freely throughout the entire prison and find out about all of these things that we're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After the bombing, we were able to move around throughout the prison, just not near to the walls because there was an order which said that anyone who got too close to the wall would be shot. But within the walls, we would move freely or semi-freely. And then there we had contact with all the prisoners and could find about -- all the prisoners told about their friends and what had happened to their friends and relatives and people around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page four, passage 3, you said that the guards told the other prisoners to help the other prisoners who were in block C. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This only happened on the 19th, when the guards fled from C block and told the other prisoners to help their fellow inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the substance of this help?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were -- only that those of us who were in isolation could go out and move freely like the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So only the people who were in isolation were able to move about. Did I understand you properly or is this something about this transcript that is not quite right?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Those who were out in freedom could move more freely than we could, but then when we were released from isolation, we could wander around the complex freely like them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many bombs hit on the 21st of May, which as you claim was quite extensive?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know of 24 projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many bombs were thrown?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You do not understand what I said. I said 24 projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say in your statement: "Two days later on the 21st of May the prison was again bombed. It started around 10.30 a.m. The guardians told the prisoners to leave the cell blocks and to remain outside in the open spaces. The guardians then left and went outside the compound again. "I could see the planes above the prison and see the bombs and rockets come from them. Buildings were hit and the bombs and rockets hit the concrete areas. Large lumps of concrete were flung into the air. One bomb fell on the concrete about 25 metres from the theatre and 16 prisoners were killed immediately by the explosion and the falling concrete. They had been in the area between the theatre." And then you speak about how you wrote the word "Help" on the ground and then you continue. "The bombing lasted all day into the evening with a break between 2.00 p.m. to 4.00 p.m. Then bombing resumed for an hour until 5.00 p.m.," and so on. And then you say: "Approximately 24 bombs fell." So the bombardment lasted all day, and you were counting precisely and determined there were 24 bombs. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is also true then that the guards of the prison, at the start of the bombardment that day, released all the prisoners from the cells and allowed them to be out in the open in order to protect themselves? Is this true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As I showed on this picture, we were staying in this prison yard that is in the centre of the complex. And when the bombing started, one bomb fell on the asphalt near the theatre, and there were great chunks of concrete that flew in the air. And there were some people who were struck by these lumps of concrete. And 16 were killed and then three died later, making 19 in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You're talking about those who were killed outside. Do you know how many prisoners remained within the prison compound during the NATO bombardment of the prison? And how many of them were killed inside the compound buildings, not those who were killed outside?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In the prison buildings, only four were killed. In the reception block where there were 167 prisoners from Gjakove who were taken hostage, and then at the entrance gate there were four killed. So if you add them together, they make 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What hostages? I don't understand. You're bringing in something new. Who was kept as a hostage?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, two buses came from Gjakove filled with people, civilians, who had been taken hostages in the town. They were taken from their shops and houses all over the city and brought to Dubrava. And as you yourself know, there was more than 1.000 people who were convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The number of inmates is not something I'm asking you about right now. I'm asking you what hostages are you talking about in the prison? I understand the people who were under investigation or people who were sentenced. What are these hostages that you are talking about in the prison? How can you have hostages in prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As I said, they were taken from the town. They were separated from their families. Their families were sent to Albania. And these people were brought to Dubrava. They were not even indicted. They were only charged and sentenced after the war was over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Krasniqi, I don't understand the number 19. You said 16 people died outside and you said also there are four people who died inside the prison building. That will make 20. Could you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all there were 19 killed, including those four. And then the number rose. One died on the way to the hospital in Peja. There were two others who were wounded that day and who are considered missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on the events which happened on the 21st. You mentioned 16 persons. Are they ones who died outside because of the bombing in the prison yard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And apart from them, there are four persons who died, who were killed inside the prison building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, these four of what we called the group from Gjakove, they were killed by the door of what we call the reception block. And then the bomb fell here, and these other prisoners were killed here in the yard. So in all, they make 19. So if you add them together, it makes 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said that there are three persons who died on 19th of May at the first bombing. So 16 plus three makes 19, and plus four makes 23. Is that your mathematics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-three were killed altogether by NATO bombing on the two different occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the deputy prison warden was killed on that occasion, also an Albanian, Nexhmedin Kalcadinaj. And also Katanja Repanovic was injured, Radomir Dobric an instructor, an electrician, Zvonko Djurovic, a driver, Milos Rajic. They were all killed or wounded. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have heard from several former prisoners who were on work details outside the prison. I've heard from them that seven Serbs were killed and also that some Albanians were killed by Serbs in order to obliterate the evidence of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is part of your story, not a fact. Tell me, during the bombing, was part of the outside wall of the prison destroyed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Only part of the sports hall where the Serbs committed these crimes. Only part of this was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether part of the outside wall of the prison was destroyed. Did a NATO rocket hit part of the outside wall of the prison and destroy it?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The wall was not fully destroyed in any part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just try and concentrate on the question. Was part of the wall destroyed or damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was only a hole about 50 centimetres square.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Give me an answer before I ask you about these 50 or 15 square centimetres. How many prisoners tried to flee from the prison through that hole on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A small number of people tried, but they were not able.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at these photographs. Let me just get one out first. You say that that is 15 square centimetres, part of the prison wall. That's what you said. And then the others, you can show all of them one after the other. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put them on the ELMO. You don't have to give them to him. Just put them on the ELMO one after the other. First the one with the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, take a look at this. Just a minute. I can't see it here. Ah, yes. Right. As you can see, part of the outside wall of the prison was hit, and a bus can go through that. It's not 15 centimetres. Do you think this was done intentionally because there were terrorists like you who were in prison? Was this done in order to make it possible for them to escape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first question, the first question is this for the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: by the bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph of the NATO complex, not of the prison, Kotllana. You can see that on the earlier photograph. There's 11 hectares of land there and that was broken by the NATO bombing. But it wasn't part of the prison complex here. You can see that on the other photograph earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's look at the other photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. The wall continues up that way. About 11 hectares of land are encircled by this wall. And that's where the wall was broken through by the bombing which you can see in the other picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the outside wall of the prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He said it's not the outside wall of the prison. That's the point. Do you want him to look at some other pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show these photographs in order. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see here the building at the entrance that was damaged; is that right? Please go ahead. Please continue. Let's save time. Go ahead. Go ahead. Let's go on. We want to have this entire set of photographs shown. And they only partly show all of this. This is the administration building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Do you recognise these buildings, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the directorate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let the caption be shown too, please. Could you place it that way on the ELMO so that the caption can also be shown? Before we saw the great damage inflicted by the bombing on the interior. Please just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see the caption, please. Could somebody translate that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "A close-up --" it says, "A close-up of the point of impact of the projectile at the pavilion of the KPD Dubrava," KPD meaning the house of corrections in Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you always place the photographs so at that we can see the captions as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't very easy for the usher, but I hope she's doing her best. I'm sure she is. You can manage? Just show the rest of the photographs if you would. Yes. Let's see them on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show all the photographs. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the caption --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same place. The point of impact of a projectile, one of the pavilions of the KPD Dubrava. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is inside. This is a point of impact of a projectile inside in the pavilion. The sky can be seen above, and also the reinforced concrete, the reinforcements from inside the concrete. Please go ahead. This is a pavilion where several prisoners lost their lives. That's what it says down here. One of the bombed facilities. Please go ahead. We have all these photographs here, and we also have corpses that were buried under the rubble. This is also in one of the cells. This is also inside. Victims that were halfway under the rubble or entirely underneath the rubble. Please go on. Here you can also see parts of human bodies in all this rubble of concrete, furniture. Please go on. Again a killed prisoner in the rubble of the KP Dom Dubrava. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's it. Do you -- just -- wait a minute. I'll ask the witness this: Do you recognise those scenes? It's been said that those were scenes which were taken no doubt after the bombing. Do you recognise them, Mr. Krasniqi, or do you want to say anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I also say -- want to say that I recognise them. And those killed on the 22nd of May, we carried them away and put them in the basement of C block, and most of these photographs were taken after we were transferred to Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you want those photographs exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means they should be exhibited. But I should like to suggest that you take a look at them, because on the overhead projector, all of it is blurred. The photographs are much clearer than from you could see on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I am going to ask for them when I need them again for another cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. They should be -- they should be exhibited now with the next exhibit number, and we will look at them during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be given Defence Exhibit 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you clip them together, put them an exhibit number on them, and then hand them to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue with my questions, I would like to introduce another document here. I would like to exhibit it. This is a record of the on-site investigation by the team from the District Court in Pec headed by Judge Vladan S. Bojic at 12.45 on the 21st of May. And then on the 24th of May at 1445 hours. And then on the 25th of May as well. Three times they had to interrupt their on-site investigation because precisely day after day there were bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking the witness now: Here in the last part at the end of the on-site investigation, it says: "From the KP Dom, a total of 93 corpses were carried out after all the crime investigation activities were carried out, I ordered the burial of the corpses as stipulated by law. I also ordered photographs to be taken before that and also the daptaloscopy [phoen] of each and every corpse. I also ordered the external examination of the corpses which was carried out by Dr. M. Stiljic [phoen], a general surgeon employed in the hospital in Pec. The entire process went on until the 26th of May until 10.00 a.m. All the identified traces of the mentioned event were in keeping with the objective circumstances marked and identified in the appropriate way. The documentation consists -- comprises part of this document, and it says District Court in Pec, the 21st, 24th, 25th, 26th of May, 1999." There is a number. There is a signature of the judge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they did not have a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a report concerning the on-site investigation that the District Court in charge carried out in relation to this crime that was committed against the prison in Dubrava by the NATO pact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asking for that to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. I would like you to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was done then when this actually happened. It was done by the appropriate judicial authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just don't know if this is the appropriate time to have this document introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but why not mark it for identification? You can then have it, the Prosecution can look at it, and if there is any objection it, you can make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just going to say before it's marked as a full exhibit. It doesn't assist with this witness because he left on the 24th and much of this is report that were done later is my point. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're fairly broad in our Rules of Evidence, so we may admit it, but subject to any objection that you want to make when you've had it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Defence Exhibit 30 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the bombing and due to the bombing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. It's time for the adjournment. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just before the adjournment, it occurs to us that if it's at all possible, the Prosecution would like to call Jacky Rowland to and have her finished if that's at all possible. I don't know -- yes. And the issue that perhaps the Court may want to consider during the break as to whether or not her evidence can be 92 bis'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had an opportunity to consider that, and the evidence will be admitted under 92 bis. The accused will have about half an hour more, so time is rather against that. We may be able to see -- you may want to see whether she can come tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the bombing 196 inmates were wounded likely or more seriously?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that about 40 of them were in a life-threatening state?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if any representatives of the authorities, the Yugoslav authorities or of the Republic of Serbia, toured the location on that day when the bombing occurred?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: What date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. No one was there on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the same day the Dubrava Prison was visited by local and international press people? What day was that according to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That was on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd. So the prison was toured after that alleged attack by the guards against the prisoners. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. After they put us into the gymnasium, Serb journalists and one Greek journalist came, but we didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after they did all of the things you said they did, they brought local and international journalists and also the representatives of the authorities also came and toured the prison. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about government representatives. I just know about the journalists and about prison personnel who were in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the next day, the 22nd of May, at one point you found yourself outside of the prison walls. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: But within the complex. Not outside the external walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that on that occasion, you recognised one of the Serb inmates who was a refugee from Albania whose name was Dritan Matanaj, which is an Albanian name, and who changed his name to Svetlan Matanovic. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I had known him earlier, but before the 22nd of May, the Serbs armed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you know what his name was, that he was a refugee from Albania, that he changed his name? How do you know all of this information?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I had spoken to him several times, because he was sentenced for criminal activities in Decan, in this town of Decan. Everyone knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why were you outside the prison walls? Did you try to escape?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't say that we were outside the prison walls. We were outside of our cells but within the prison complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what it states in your statement, but let's not waste time on that now. How many prisoners tried to escape from the prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A very small number, but they were not successful in their attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were they prevented?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From the hole we talked about earlier, which was caused by the NATO bombing, through that hole in the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this was from -- the size of the hole was from 15 to 50 square centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: 50 centimetres, not 15, because 50 you can get through. There was a wall with bricks, and you could take some of the bricks -- they could take some of the bricks out and make it bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Ten by ten centimetres gives 100 square centimetres. So I don't know if anybody can pass through a hole like that, through one square decametre.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Through 50 square centimetres you could get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was there bombing by NATO on the 22nd of May of the Dubrava Prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. The day before, on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that over 90 bodies of killed prisoners were pulled out from the rubble of the prison buildings?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We left for the prison in Lipjan, and they could of course do anything they wanted, stage anything they wanted after that because we couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that you saw and that is quite enough. Do you know that another 90 prisoners were killed in -- died in hospitals in subsequent days as a direct consequence of the NATO bombing of the prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I only know of one prisoner who died in hospital, and that was on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So in spite of your description about the bombing which lasted over several days giving the impression that the prison buildings were practically razed to the ground, you still claim that the prisoners were killed by the prison guards. How is this possible? Why are you not speaking the truth?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: If you could show the photograph once again of the complex, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have time now to look at those photographs. Our time is limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him explain. You've put to him he's lying, so he should have the opportunity to explain. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the bombing on the 21st, we were here in the yard, around the complex. One witness -- or one prisoner, rather, was on the sports field, and he said, "Come on over this way to the sports field because we're going to bomb the buildings." So all of us, we ran through the buildings -- between the buildings and came down to the sports field, and that's how we survived the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In spite of this bombing which went on for several days and a large number of victims, and in spite of your claim that this was not a consequence of the NATO bombing but an act committed by the guards, you have just described that you were showered by hand grenades, fire from automatic rifles, a bazooka, and so on. And then they suddenly gave up on their intention to kill you. And you also claim that you, even though through the efforts of Judge Kwon you stated that about 20 people were firing, you used the opportunity while they were changing their cartridges to run away. As an instructor of the KLA terrorists, you know that if 20 people are firing at the same time, even if they are ordered to do so, they would not be able to replace their ammunition at the same time. Isn't this true? Why did you make this up?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know that according to military regulations soldiers are supposed to listen to their officers, listen to the orders given to them their officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If that is your explanation, then that is quite sufficient. Could you please tell me, how is it possible? Your description of the events is that they tried with all of those automatic weapons, and the bazooka and the hand grenades, they were trying to kill you, and then after that 800 of you are driven by buses and trucks to a different prison or to different prisons. You are evacuated in order to save you. What prevented them from killing you if they had the intention of killing you? You didn't run away. Isn't that right? You stayed there. They gathered you up again and then they moved you to a different place in buses and trucks. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were at the sports field and then the soldiers and the paramilitaries came in and told us that -- they told us that there was a -- that there had been a catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And while being seen by those soldiers and the police officers and the prison guards, you burned your own documents at your own initiative, allegedly so that you would not be beaten because you had documents on you. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This was so that documents would not be found on us in Serbia and so that we would be identified as having been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you were being taken to prison, then it's an assumption that you were convicted. There must have been some records about you or do you think that there were no records and that it was only a question of your own personal documents?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nobody asked whether we were convicted or not convicted. Any Albanian was a terrorist. And this was -- and the guards and the soldiers transferred whom they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I wasn't asking you that. Can you please tell me, at the end of the NATO bombing, did any prison buildings remain standing or were they all destroyed in the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Only the sports hall was left. And also, as you can see in the photograph, it was destroyed in the -- in the school room and the library. It was demolished by the Serbs themselves who threw hand grenades in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please tell me now if on the 24th of May the prison warden and a few guards came to the prisoners and brought you water, cartons of cigarettes, food, and so on? You say that on page 7 in paragraph 4. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. This was not right. This happened on the 23rd. And they gave us cigarettes in the name of a certain Miki who was the head of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the day on which they, as you say, were killing you?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They lined us up on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the day before they were ruthlessly killing you, and the next day they brought you cigarettes, food, and informed you that you would be evacuated. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That was their job, and that is still their job today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, since you were keeping a record as if you were the prison warden, how many prisoners in total were transported in trucks and buses? You said eight buses and four trucks. The number is not important, the number of buses and trucks, but how many prisoners were transported, evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said eight buses and four trucks, and beyond that I can't speak with any authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. According to a report or information about the NATO attack by the Ministry of Justice which is responsible for the prisoners, so I have information that 800 of you were evacuated to other prisons. Is that the figure approximately or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Approximately. Seven hundred and seventy is my number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And four days later, another 24 persons were brought to the Dubrava and Lipjan Prison.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's a mistake. They brought 24 more to Lipjan, but after that we didn't see them at all, and these people are now counted missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this evacuation from the location that was bombed, did that save the lives of many prisoners? Eight hundred of you were evacuated to other prisons. So yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Could you put that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether the evacuation, you were evacuated in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these eight buses and four trucks and so on, did that evacuation save your lives, the lives of those 800 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were two possibilities, because there were -- you could no longer stay in the complex because there was no water, there was no food, and everything was rendered unusable, and that's why they sent us to Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the prison was bombed after the 24th of May, after you were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know about that. After the 24th, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you explained that anti-aircraft defence fired shots in order to provoke the NATO aeroplanes. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said that they did indeed provoke the NATO aircraft from outside the prison walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider it a provocation if somebody fires at fighting aircraft, in this case of a foreign power, that is attacking your country? And if they are defending themselves and using anti-aircraft weapons, do you consider that could be a provocation?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were plenty of places they could have carried out this provocation rather than by a prison, and the intention was to attract NATO to kill us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, time is coming to an end. Two more questions if you want to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This twisted logic of yours that anti-aircraft defence from NATO aggression constitutes a provocation and this tale of yours that during the several days of bombing by NATO which you yourself partially described, the victims were not caused by NATO bombing but allegedly by the acts of the guards, the very guards who actually saved you by evacuating you from that place, 800 of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is a speech. You've already put that question. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Indeed I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krasniqi, in your statement that you gave before, you said that you had been arrested while driving together with your family towards Rozaje, and today you said that was not correct, that as a matter of fact, you were ambushed. Can you explain this ambush to us, what kind of an ambush this was? Were you armed at the moment you were ambushed or were you in any kind of action related to KLA activity? Could you explain all of that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't say that I was armed during an ambush. I said I was with my family. There were collaborators working, Albanian collaborators who were working for Serbia, who were involved, and that's what I would call an ambush or a trap.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that it was some other Albanians who had prepared your arrest?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. They were Albanian -- they were Albanians who were working for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said today that the Serb authorities had information that you were a commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Among those who organised this ambush, there were people who did have such information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You really were a commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not from the 1st of September on. I returned to my profession as a schoolteacher and worked as a schoolteacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But for a while you were a commander. And the proceedings that took place against you, you said earlier on over here that you did not admit in these proceedings that you had been a commander, that you only admitted to having been a member of the KLA and that is why you were sentenced to one year in prison only.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior was aware of everything I had done, where as the legal authorities at the trial remained silent on that. Otherwise, I wouldn't be alive today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were sentenced only on account of what you admitted. You did not admit to that which was higher, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't admit anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I have to point out to you that you said here on page 1 of your statement, paragraph 9, you said that you did admit to being a member of the KLA but not that you were a commander. That's what you did say in your statement earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Laws in Serbia are quite elastic. They asked me during the investigation what I had done. I accepted that I had been working for the KLA, but the investigators remained silent on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you just give me brief answers to my questions. You said awhile ago that in that prison in Dubrava there were about 1.000 Albanians for the most part, or was it Albanians only?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were mostly Albanians. There were very few who were Serbs. Seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give a rough estimate at least of how many Serbs there were? Oh, yes. I see. Thank you. Out of these Albanians who were in prison, were most of them members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A very small part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yesterday or, as a matter of fact, today, you said that there were cases when people were beaten. But before the 21st of May, were any Albanians endangered in such a way that their actual lives were in danger? Was there a single Albanian who had lost his or her life before the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, that's the reason why I didn't admit for having worked for the KLA, because I knew I would have been killed. I would have been murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether anybody was killed in prison before the 21st -- or the 19th of May, rather. That is my question. And all of these men were ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Deaths, no, but there were all different types of mistreatments and mishandling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody killed after being transferred to prisons in Serbia? You were transferred to Pozarevac. Further on in these prisons were any of these Albanians killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There certainly were people killed, but I don't know of any names because it was earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In prison? You know that somebody was killed while you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I heard that people had been killed at the prison in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which prison in Nis? Do you know the name? You didn't refer to that earlier at all.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: KP Dom Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested in in relation to your statement is the following: The day when you were told that you would be transferred to the prison in Nis, you said earlier on: "Some prisoners who came from Nis said that we should burn or destroy," that's what you said today, "our personal documents." And then you explained why this was necessary. So this was an agreement reached amongst you yourselves, the prisoners. That is what the prisoners had suggested.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, because of the bitter experience that they had had there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you burned that? How could you get fire in a prison and how could you burn documents? That is one question.

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were prisoners, ordinary prisoners, who had been accused, who had been sentenced for ordinary crimes. They had small tools. They had pencils. They had razors, radios, lighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's no interpretation. I don't have any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Some of the prisoners had been sentenced for ordinary crimes. They had razors, radios, and lighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is the following: Since they were in prison, how did they manage to burn documents? How could they make a fire in prison when there were so many prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, he has explained it. He said some of them had lighters. Now we really must try and move on. I don't want to hurry you, but we really must try and move on. We've spent nearly two or three hours with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always hurry, and I will certainly stop altogether if you tell me to do so, but I'm interested in the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Prisoners in prison never have any documents of their own on them. They have to hand over everything they have to the prison authorities when they enter prison. How come that all of them had their own documents on them? Can he explain that first? Or can he explain how they managed to obtain their documents if they had been taken away from them beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I had the sentence, my sentence, and that is what I burnt, the document I was sentenced by. And in the accusation it said that I had been accused of various crimes, and that's what I burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the following: When you were taken out in front of the buildings where you were staying and when you were told that you would be transferred to Nis, did people accept that or did they think that they should not leave Kosovo and the prison in Kosovo and that they didn't want to go to Serbia? Was there any kind of resistance in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They told us twice that we would be going to Nis. On the 22nd and then on the 23rd. That's the time you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I mean. But did you accept that or did you resist this proposal altogether since you were supposed to be transferred to the territory of Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were in prison. We had no choice about the matter whether -- as to go or not to go. We had our hands tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The bombing that followed, as you had put it, on the 19th of May, but in your statement you refer to the time between the 24th of March and the 21st of May, and you said that NATO aircraft, or, rather, that you often saw NATO aircraft in the sky and also that there was bombing around Istok. How far away is Istok from the prison? And before the 19th of May, how often did you hear the area surrounding the prison being bombed?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They bombed the prison, around the prison, several times but from a 2 kilometre altitude and around Istog. But it is wasn't in May, as you said, but it was the middle of April. There were provocations on the part of Serb forces. They were using anti-aircraft equipment, weapons, to shoot at the NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many bombs fell then? Could you tell by the explosions?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, Serb forces provoked NATO all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be interesting, but I wonder how relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, Mr. Tapuskovic. Could you kindly finish, please, though, in four minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tanks, armoured vehicles, anti-aircraft guns were in front of the prison. They were not within the prison compound?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As I said, they were near Kotllana and around the directorate of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand it when you were speaking about this today. You never mentioned in your statement before that NATO bombs had hit this equipment, these weapons. Today you said that they were destroyed, right, or did you not say that?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't mention that in my statement because no one asked me about it. I said that on the 24th, they extradited us to Lipjan, and we saw that equipment had been destroyed by the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't say that before. I have two more topics. In that bombing, the people you saw being killed, did they have external injuries on their bodies? Was it obvious that they were injured, that their bodies were injured by the bombs that fell? Did they have visible injuries?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You saw people who were killed. Were there visible injuries on their bodies? Were there visible injuries showing that they had been hit?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Do you mean injuries from NATO or from Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From shelling, bullets. Generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were a lot who were injured. A lot of people were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But those who had lost their lives, did their bodies have any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. visible wounds, injuries on them?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that for the following reason: Did you see anybody who died without having sustained any visible external injuries? Were there any persons who died who had not sustained any external visible injuries?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From what I heard from my -- the other people, there were two people who died in that manner, but I don't know. Who didn't -- people who didn't have any external injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that 23 persons lost their lives without having any external visible injuries because their lungs simply broke due to the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's not true at all. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, if you don't know. Thank you. My last question has to do with the following: In your statement, you said that "What happened when the bombs were falling was a horrifying experience. We could only pray that the bombs and rockets would not fall and explode around us." So you were very frightened of them, weren't you? Did you feel any fear? Was it indeed a horrifying experience, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: If NATO had destroyed, had killed all of us, we would have been happy about it. Nine hundred prisoners in the prison. We would all have been happy if they had killed us if they had only one, destroyed everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, if I could ask first so that you can have an opportunity to clarify later. Mr. Krasniqi, if my memory is correct that I remember that you said that the total number of prisoners who lined up in the early morning of 22nd was up to 800. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then all of a sudden there came throwing of grenades and shooting from 20 people or something like that. Could you give us your estimate of the total number of prisoners who were killed at that time by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- during that incident when we were lined up, I would say 97 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I hadn't intended to ask any questions, but I should because of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you said that about 800 lined up, did you also tell us earlier in chief that not all the prisoners of the 930 prisoners or some odd that you thought were there were actually on the sports field, that some had actually hidden in other locations within the prison? Did I understand you correctly to say that?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So there were about a hundred or more prisoners who were not lined up on the sports field on the early morning hours of the 22nd of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not all were lined up. There were still some in the cell blocks. There were some who were still sleeping. There were some in different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are all the questions I have but there is one further housekeeping matter if I may, Your Honour, and that is that the second photograph that had been attached to the statement, the statement is not an exhibit, but the photograph -- I'm sorry. I guess it's sort of his handwritten one. That should be marked as an exhibit as well if I may and we have additional copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is at the door so if the usher could perhaps take this witness out, but bring the next witness in before she takes him back to the witness room. I would be grateful to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the position about this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She can stay tomorrow, but in fact, we certainly can deal with her evidence in chief via the mechanism of 92 bis and perhaps and probably more this morning. This evidence will be very short

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have got quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are not in a position to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, your full name?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND
utterances.text: My full name is Jacklin Debra Rowland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you a BBC journalist?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make a statement to the Office of the Prosecution of an interview on the 14th of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you here yesterday, before an officer of the Tribunal attest to the accuracy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that statement and the associated documentation be produced as an exhibit? Two short video extracts to be played within the summary that I am going to read out. I think the booth is ready to play them and I'll tell them when I want them to be played. The summary of this witness's evidence is as follows: That as a 38-year-old journalist who works for the British Broadcasting Corporation, she worked in 1998 and 1999 in Belgrade and in Kosovo, during which time she visited many locations including Dubrava Prison in Istok municipality. Two such visits of which the first was on the 21st of May, 1999, when the witness visited Dubrava Prison with a film crew, interpreters, and other international journalists. That group was met by a man who identified himself as the governor of the prison and by an investigating judge. The judge commented that he was not sure what was going on inside the prison, that there was some panic, that some prisoners had escaped from their cells and others had been released by guards on humanitarian grounds. The investigating judge told the group that NATO had bombed the prison and killed several prisoners. Inside the prison, Ms. Rowland noted number of bodies, less than 20 she observed, lying in different locations outside the prison buildings. The bodies appeared to be wearing civilian clothing and the witness noted that the prison had not been greatly damaged but in the area she was given access to a perimeter call had been breached. She also saw a hundred prisoners lined up near a perimeter wall held at gunpoint by guards who were wearing blue uniforms. She noted one guard was armed with what appeared to be a Kalashnikov and was wearing a green quilted vest, black baseball cap, hat, dark shirt and dark trousers. She filed a report based on her observations. And if the room would be good enough, please, the video room, to play the first extract, which is the report she filed for television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: JACKY ROWLAND: This was a civilian target say the Serb officials who brought us here. For two hours this morning, NATO pounded this gaol firing about 15 missiles into the main complex and blowing a hole in the perimeter wall. INVESTIGATING JUDGE: This is the second time NATO has attacked this gaol. I can't find words to describe what I think. JACKY ROWLAND: We were told that the prison houses convicted thieves, rapists and other criminals but what makes Istok gaol interesting is that among its inmates are members of the Kosovo Liberation Army. The authorities say a thousand prisoners are being held here. The inmates have been let out of their cells. You can see them behind me lined up against the wall. Some of them have been killed in the NATO attack. Others may have escaped. By unlocking the cells the guards thought they'd give the prisoners a better chance of survival. For many this gamble didn't pay off. We were told at least ten people had been killed in this first wave of bombing, but that wasn't the end of the story. The drone of bombers could still be heard overhead and as we raced away from the scene, NATO struck again. There was clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, just pausing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Ms. Rowland, the first person interviewed with the curly hair was the investigating judge, and the person with the green quilted vest you referred to was the man we saw towards the end of the clip with an AK-47 and what appeared to be a pistol in the other hand?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The summary continues. On the 24th of May, 1999, Ms. Rowland visited the prison on a second occasion with other journalists and a film crew. The investigating judge, the same man, was on site but not the governor. The witness observed that the prison had been badly damaged in the preceding few days and that there appeared to be no living prisoners in the prison. She was told that NATO had bombed the prison all weekend and that all the prisoners had been removed. Her evidence is that even though the prison was deserted, she and other journalists were not allowed to move freely about the compound but were escorted and only taken to certain locations. She noted that the guards present on this occasion were dressed in green camouflage uniforms with Balaclava masks and observed, did Ms. Rowland, 44 dead prisoners outside prison buildings, many under blankets, her assessment being that this number included the bodies she had seen on a previous witness which appeared to be left in situ. She also saw 25 bodies piled inside a building. These people did not appear to have died in the building, and the witness concluded that they'd been moved to this location after death, observing that many had their trousers pulled down to their knees exposing their underwear. All the bodies appearing had been dead for more than one day because their skin started to change colour. She also noted there were sandbags on the roof of a small building close to the prison but outside its perimeter walls. She filed another report. May we see the second part of this video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: JACKY ROWLAND: Our latest visit to Istok prison poses more questions than it offers answers. It's clear that the prison has been badly pounded by NATO since our first visit on Friday. One building was smouldering while the dining room several cellblocks were badly damaged. The authorities say tens of people have been killed in the bombing raids and about 200 injured. They say bombers have been circling overhead for days making it impossible to remove the dead and wounded. According to the police, the prison was finally evacuated early on Monday. Walking around the prison we counted 44 bodies. About half these appeared to be the victims of the first bombing raid on Friday, still lying under blankets on the grass. Then we were taken to a room in a damaged cellblock where there were 25 corpses. INVESTIGATING JUDGE: On this site was committed the most horrific loss of life. There was a large number of casualties who were transferred to the nearest hospital. The investigation is ongoing. JACKY ROWLAND: We were told they had died between Friday and Sunday, although it was not clear how all of them had met their death nor why they were all in one relatively undamaged room. It's difficult to assess exactly what is the significance of Istok prison, although NATO has described it as a military and police context. Jacky Rowland, BBC, Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes the summary, Your Honour. The video which we've been playing is a composition of extracts from K991. May it be given a separate exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. First of all the statement, secondly the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 291, and the video will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I noticed that in this package, there are two statements that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason for that is the one that was presented for signature to Ms. Rowland didn't have a caption or a footing on it. She signed that. The other one is identical but is simply the original statement that she signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for cross-examination. Ms. Rowland, I understand that you can back tomorrow for cross-examination. Thank you for making yourself available. Nine o'clock, please. We will continue with your evidence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you rise, the witness immediately following Ms. Rowland is a Mrs. Imeraj. I know there have been some difficulties about the mechanics of having her statement and addendum bis'd, but I'm hopeful that maybe subject to that process this afternoon, we would be grateful at some stage for an indication, obviously, as to whether that process will be acceptable in her case. I think she is the first person to deal with this particular massacre. Of course it's always a question of degree, to what degree things are a repetition of other events or a part of other events or are unique to themselves. So it's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will look at her evidence and we'll let you know tomorrow. Ms. Rowland, there's one other matter I should tell you formally that since your evidence has started, don't speak to anybody about it, please, until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
